title: To the Waters: you are the bringers of well-being

words.context: Bhāskara: «आपः व्यापितास्», the Waters as what pervades

words.role: gives the ground of the request
words.context: Sāyaṇa on the Ṛgveda: «हि यस्मात् कारणात्», ‘because’

words.gram: present indicative, 2nd pl. active (pada form स्थ)
words.context: after hi the s becomes ṣ and the final a is lengthened in the Saṃhitā; the pada text has स्थ

words.meaning: bringers of well-being, sources of joy

words.role: takes up āpaḥ as subject of dadhātana

words.meaning: for delight, for what is lovely

samasa.type: upapada (a noun with a verbal root as the second member)
samasa.meaning: those who bring joy into being

morphology.note: the verb स्थ, ‘you are’, as the Saṃhitā recites it after हि: the s is retroflexed and the final vowel lengthened. The word division keeps the recited form.
the old Vedic imperative ending -tana for -ta (classical दधात).

translation.literal: O Waters, you are indeed bringers of well-being; such, set us towards nourishment, towards great delightful seeing.
translation.readable: Waters, you are the source of well-being: give us strength, and the joy of seeing clearly.

words.role: opens the relative clause, with rasaḥ
partitive object of bhājayata: ‘give us a share of it’

sandhi.rule: visarga after a vowel other than a or ā becomes r before a vowel

morphology.note: the Vedic feminine plural in -īḥ of the present participle of √वश् ‘to desire’.

translation.literal: Which sap of yours is most kindly, of that make us share here, like loving mothers.
translation.readable: Give us here a share of your most kindly essence, as loving mothers give to their children.

words.role: goal of gamāma: the sap of the previous verse

words.meaning: may we go, let us come
words.role: main verb of the first line

words.meaning: for the abode, for the dwelling

words.gram: present indicative/imperative, 2nd pl. active (pada form जनयथ)
words.context: Sāyaṇa: «नोऽस्माञ्जनयथ प्रजोत्पादकन्कुरुथ», ‘make us able to beget offspring’

words.role: joins the request to the previous clause

sandhi.rule: -ai before a vowel becomes -āy, and the y is dropped, leaving a hiatus

morphology.note: the final a of जनयथ is lengthened in the Saṃhitā of a ṛk (P. 6.3.133 (ऋचि तुनुघमक्षुतङ्कुत्रोरुष्याणाम्) lists such lengthenings); the word division keeps the recited form.
a root aorist subjunctive of √गम्: ‘let us go’.

translation.literal: To that may we go fully, to you, for whose dwelling you are pleased; and, O Waters, generate us.
translation.readable: May we come fully to that essence of yours, in whose abode you delight; and, Waters, give us life and offspring.

meaning: Three short ṛks addressed to the Waters, the most recited verses of the Sandhyāvandanam. The Waters are asked for three things: strength and clear sight, a share of their kindly essence, and new life. The second verse compares them to loving mothers who give of themselves to their children. In the Taittirīya Saṃhitā (4.1.5.1) the verses are said while water is poured on the clay of the fire-pan, to cool the fire’s heat — Sāyaṇa cites the Brāhmaṇa’s instruction «तिसृभिरुप सृजति». The same three ṛks open hymn 10.9 of the Ṛgveda. In the rite they accompany the sprinkling of water on the head: what cooled the fire is now asked to cool and purify the worshipper.
in_the_rite: Mārjana: water is sprinkled on the head, verse by verse, and then round the self with the vyāhṛtis; recited again in the second mārjana after dadhikrāvṇo, in all three services. The Mylapore prayoga gives the viniyoga: Sindhudvīpa the seer, gāyatrī the metre, the Waters the deity, used for sprinkling (vin-apo-hi-stha).

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Sāyaṇa, on TS 4.1.5, places the three ṛks in the making of the fire-pan: water is mixed in to calm the fire’s heat, as the Brāhmaṇa says, «तिसृभिरुप सृजति त्रिवृद्वा अग्निर्यावानेवाग्निस्तस्य शुचँ शमयति». On the second verse he explains the simile: «कामयमानाः प्रीतियुक्ता मातरो यथा वत्सान्स्वकीयस्तन्यरसं प्रापयन्ति तद्वत्» — as loving mothers give their calves their own milk.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: On the third verse Sāyaṇa reads tasmai as ‘to that sap’ and janayatha as a prayer for offspring: «तस्मै रसाय वौ युष्मानरं गमामालं भृशं प्राप्नुमः», «हे आपो यूयं नोऽस्माञ्जनयथ प्रजोत्पादकन्कुरुथ».

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara glosses the first verse: «आपः व्यापितास् स्थ मयोभुवः सुखस्य भावयित्र्यः» — the Waters pervade, and they bring well-being; ūrje is ‘for sap’ (or ‘give us strength’), and the great delightful seeing is knowledge: «चक्षसे ज्ञानाय».

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Sāyaṇa on the Ṛgveda (10.9.1) takes hi as ‘because’ and draws the same reading of the last line towards insight: «अस्मान् सम्यग्ज्ञानं प्रति यौग्यान् कुरुतेत्यर्थः».

notes.label: linguistic
notes.text: Gāyatrī metre: three pādas of eight syllables per ṛk. The Ṛgveda (10.9.1–3) has the same words; the Taittirīya differs only in spelling (वश्शिवतमः for वः शिवतमः, अरङ्गमाम for अरं गमाम).

notes.label: traditional
notes.text: In the Saṃhitā these verses calm the fire; in the rite they are said with water on the head. The prayoga’s viniyoga names Sindhudvīpa as the seer.
